section.title: Alternating products: a first glimpse of forms
section.p: The determinant gave us signed area and signed volume. That sign was not decoration. It was the whole point. When we swapped two directions, the parallelogram stayed the same, but its orientation reversed: \det[\mathbf u\ \mathbf v]=-\det[\mathbf v\ \mathbf u]. Now we give that sign-changing behavior a name. It is the first step toward differential forms.

subsection.title: Area as a bilinear alternating measurement
subsection.p: A carpenter lays a small slanted tile on the floor. One side of the tile follows the vector \mathbf u=(3,1), and the adjacent side follows \mathbf v=(1,2). The signed area of the parallelogram is \det[\mathbf u\ \mathbf v]=\begin{vmatrix}3&1\\1&2\end{vmatrix}=3\cdot2-1\cdot1=5.
The tile has ordinary area 5. It also has positive orientation because the ordered pair \mathbf u,\mathbf v turns counterclockwise.

If we walk around the same tile in the opposite order, the signed area becomes \det[\mathbf v\ \mathbf u]=\begin{vmatrix}1&3\\2&1\end{vmatrix}=1\cdot1-2\cdot3=-5. The tile did not shrink. Only the orientation changed.

figure.caption: The same parallelogram has opposite signed area when the order is reversed.

subsection.p:
The determinant also behaves linearly in each input. For example, split \mathbf u=(3,1) into \mathbf u=(3,0)+(0,1). Then
\det[(3,1)\ \mathbf v]\amp=\det[(3,0)\ \mathbf v]+\det[(0,1)\ \mathbf v].
With \mathbf v=(1,2), this says 5=\begin{vmatrix}3&1\\0&2\end{vmatrix}+\begin{vmatrix}0&1\\1&2\end{vmatrix}=6+(-1). So signed area is additive in the first vector. It is also additive in the second vector. Stretch one side by a factor of c, and the signed area is stretched by the same factor.
This is the pattern.

exercise.title: Why do repeated vector inputs give zero?

statement.p: The word alternating means that swapping the two inputs reverses the sign: B(\mathbf v,\mathbf u)=-B(\mathbf u,\mathbf v). Think about what this says geometrically for a parallelogram's signed area, and then explain why feeding the same vector into both slots of this real-valued measurement must give zero.

hint.p: Put \mathbf u=\mathbf v into the swap rule. You get B(\mathbf u,\mathbf u)=-B(\mathbf u,\mathbf u). What is the only number equal to its own negative? Geometrically, a vector and itself span no area.

statement.p: A function B(\mathbf u,\mathbf v) that takes two vectors and returns a number is called bilinear if it is linear in each input separately: B(a\mathbf u+b\mathbf w,\mathbf v)=aB(\mathbf u,\mathbf v)+bB(\mathbf w,\mathbf v), and B(\mathbf u,a\mathbf v+b\mathbf w)=aB(\mathbf u,\mathbf v)+bB(\mathbf u,\mathbf w).
It is called alternating if swapping the two inputs changes the sign: B(\mathbf v,\mathbf u)=-B(\mathbf u,\mathbf v). In particular, B(\mathbf u,\mathbf u)=0.

subsection.p: The determinant in the plane is bilinear and alternating: \det[\mathbf u\ \mathbf v]=u_1v_2-u_2v_1.

theorem.title: Every planar alternating bilinear measurement is area times a constant

statement.p: Let B be a bilinear alternating function of two vectors in \mathbb R^2. Then there is a constant c such that \boxed{B(\mathbf u,\mathbf v)=c(u_1v_2-u_2v_1)} for all \mathbf u=(u_1,u_2),\qquad \mathbf v=(v_1,v_2). In other words, every bilinear alternating measurement in the plane is a constant multiple of signed area.

proof.p:
Let \mathbf e_1=(1,0),\qquad \mathbf e_2=(0,1). Write \mathbf u=u_1\mathbf e_1+u_2\mathbf e_2,\qquad \mathbf v=v_1\mathbf e_1+v_2\mathbf e_2. By bilinearity,
B(\mathbf u,\mathbf v)\amp=B(u_1\mathbf e_1+u_2\mathbf e_2,\, v_1\mathbf e_1+v_2\mathbf e_2) \amp=u_1v_1B(\mathbf e_1,\mathbf e_1)+u_1v_2B(\mathbf e_1,\mathbf e_2) \amp\qquad +u_2v_1B(\mathbf e_2,\mathbf e_1)+u_2v_2B(\mathbf e_2,\mathbf e_2).
Because B is alternating, B(\mathbf e_1,\mathbf e_1)=0,\qquad B(\mathbf e_2,\mathbf e_2)=0, and B(\mathbf e_2,\mathbf e_1)=-B(\mathbf e_1,\mathbf e_2). Let c=B(\mathbf e_1,\mathbf e_2). Then
B(\mathbf u,\mathbf v)\amp=u_1v_2c-u_2v_1c \amp=c(u_1v_2-u_2v_1).

subsection.p: The two hypotheses are real hypotheses.

First, bilinearity matters. Define B(\mathbf u,\mathbf v)=(u_1v_2-u_2v_1)^3. Swapping \mathbf u and \mathbf v changes the sign, so this function is alternating. But it is not bilinear. For example, B(\mathbf e_1,\mathbf e_2)=1, while B(2\mathbf e_1,\mathbf e_2)=8. A bilinear function would have given 2, not 8. So this is not a constant multiple of signed area.

Second, alternating matters. The dot product D(\mathbf u,\mathbf v)=\mathbf u\cdot\mathbf v is bilinear, but it is not alternating. Indeed, D(\mathbf e_1,\mathbf e_1)=1, while an alternating measurement must give B(\mathbf e_1,\mathbf e_1)=0. The dot product measures alignment, not oriented area.

subsection.title: The coordinate measurements dx, dy, and dz
subsection.p: The determinant formula u_1v_2-u_2v_1 has two parts. It uses the x-component of one vector and the y-component of the other, then subtracts the same measurement with the roles reversed.
To name those component measurements, we write dx(a,b)=a,\qquad dy(a,b)=b. So dx reads the x-component of a vector, and dy reads the y-component.
For example, if \mathbf u=(3,1),\qquad \mathbf v=(1,2), then dx(\mathbf u)=3,\qquad dy(\mathbf u)=1, and dx(\mathbf v)=1,\qquad dy(\mathbf v)=2.

These are the first examples of 1-forms: objects that take one vector and return one number. Later, a 1-form like P\,dx+Q\,dy will be the kind of object we integrate along a curve. For now, dx and dy are simply coordinate-measuring devices.
In space we also have dz(a,b,c)=c.

subsection.title: Why dx\,dy should not mean ordinary multiplication
subsection.p: A parallelogram has two side vectors. So an area measurement must take two vector inputs, not one.

If \mathbf u=(3,1),\qquad \mathbf v=(1,2), then ordinary multiplication might tempt us to write dx(\mathbf u)\,dy(\mathbf v)=3\cdot2=6. But the signed area is not 6. It is 3\cdot2-1\cdot1=5. The missing piece is the swapped product: dy(\mathbf u)\,dx(\mathbf v)=1\cdot1=1. Signed area is the difference: dx(\mathbf u)\,dy(\mathbf v)-dy(\mathbf u)\,dx(\mathbf v).
This difference is important enough to get its own symbol.

statement.p: More generally, let \alpha and \beta be linear functions from vectors to real numbers. Their wedge is the two-input measurement (\alpha\wedge\beta)(\mathbf u,\mathbf v)=\alpha(\mathbf u)\beta(\mathbf v)-\alpha(\mathbf v)\beta(\mathbf u). Thus \alpha and \beta each take one vector, while \alpha\wedge\beta takes an ordered pair of vectors and returns a scalar. This definition does not define a wedge of two vectors.

subsection.p: A sum or scalar multiple of measurements is evaluated by adding or scaling their values. Expanding the preceding definition therefore gives (a\alpha+b\beta)\wedge\gamma=a(\alpha\wedge\gamma)+b(\beta\wedge\gamma), and the same distributive rule in the second factor. Interchanging the two scalar products gives \beta\wedge\alpha=-\alpha\wedge\beta. In particular, \alpha\wedge\alpha=0: its value on every ordered pair is the difference of two identical products. These are identities of measurements, meaning that both sides give the same value on every pair of vectors.
So dx\wedge dy is not ordinary multiplication. The wedge symbol \wedge is a warning: \text{measure the ordered area, and subtract the swapped order.}

exercise.title: Why isn't dx\wedge dy ordinary multiplication?

statement.p: Ordinary multiplication is commutative: ab=ba. But the definition gives dx\wedge dy=-dy\wedge dx. Using the idea that dx\wedge dy measures the signed area of the parallelogram built from two ordered vectors, explain in your own words why reversing the order of dx and dy should flip the sign rather than leave it unchanged.

hint.p: Evaluate both dx\wedge dy and dy\wedge dx on the same ordered pair (\mathbf u,\mathbf v). Their two scalar products occur with opposite signs. Compare this with the effect of swapping the vector inputs.

subsection.p: This is why the notation dx\,dy is too quiet when orientation matters. In ordinary double integrals, dA often means unsigned little area. But the form dx\wedge dy remembers orientation. Reversing the order reverses the sign.

subsection.title: Coordinate shadows in space
subsection.p: A parallelogram in space casts shadows onto the coordinate planes. Each shadow has a signed area.

Let \mathbf u=(2,1,3),\qquad \mathbf v=(1,4,0). The signed area of the shadow on the xy-plane is
(dx\wedge dy)(\mathbf u,\mathbf v)\amp=\begin{vmatrix}2&1\\1&4\end{vmatrix} \amp=2\cdot4-1\cdot1 \amp=7.

The signed area of the shadow on the yz-plane is
(dy\wedge dz)(\mathbf u,\mathbf v)\amp=\begin{vmatrix}1&4\\3&0\end{vmatrix} \amp=1\cdot0-3\cdot4 \amp=-12.

The signed area of the shadow on the zx-plane is
(dz\wedge dx)(\mathbf u,\mathbf v)\amp=\begin{vmatrix}3&0\\2&1\end{vmatrix} \amp=3\cdot1-2\cdot0 \amp=3.

figure.caption: The same oriented parallelogram gives three signed coordinate shadows. Dashed segments project its vertices onto the actual coordinate planes. The order of each plane's coordinates matters: the yz-shadow has negative signed area. (Interactive: drag to rotate, scroll to zoom.)

image.shortdescription: A 3D parallelogram and true xy, yz, zx projections, joined by dashed lines and labeled with signed areas +7, -12, +3.

subsection.p: This is a beautiful fact. The cross product packages three coordinate area measurements into one vector. But the area measurements themselves are the wedge products.
That is why the wedge product survives in every dimension, while the cross product is special to three dimensions.

subsection.title: Signed volume as dx\wedge dy\wedge dz
subsection.p: The same idea works for volume.
A signed volume measurement takes three vectors. It is linear in each input and changes sign whenever two inputs are swapped.
The basic signed volume measurement in space is dx\wedge dy\wedge dz.

definition.title: The volume form dx\wedge dy\wedge dz

statement.p: For vectors \mathbf u,\mathbf v,\mathbf w\in\mathbb R^3, the form dx\wedge dy\wedge dz is defined by \boxed{(dx\wedge dy\wedge dz)(\mathbf u,\mathbf v,\mathbf w)=\det[\mathbf u\ \mathbf v\ \mathbf w].} It measures the signed volume of the parallelepiped spanned by the ordered triple \mathbf u,\mathbf v,\mathbf w.

subsection.p:
For example, let \mathbf u=(1,2,0),\qquad \mathbf v=(0,1,3),\qquad \mathbf w=(2,0,1). Then
(dx\wedge dy\wedge dz)(\mathbf u,\mathbf v,\mathbf w)\amp=\begin{vmatrix}1&0&2\\2&1&0\\0&3&1\end{vmatrix} \amp=13.
So the ordered triple spans signed volume 13.
If we swap the first two vectors, the sign flips: (dx\wedge dy\wedge dz)(\mathbf v,\mathbf u,\mathbf w)=-13. Again, the box is the same. The orientation is not.

subsection.title: Forms as future integrands
subsection.p: The word form may sound abstract, but at this stage it means something very concrete.
A 1-form measures a vector: dx,\qquad dy,\qquad P\,dx+Q\,dy. Later, 1-forms will be integrated along curves.
A 2-form measures oriented area: dx\wedge dy,\qquad dy\wedge dz,\qquad dz\wedge dx. Later, 2-forms will be integrated over surfaces and regions.
A 3-form measures oriented volume: dx\wedge dy\wedge dz. Later, 3-forms will be integrated over solids.

exercise.title: Why does an ordered pair carry a sign?

statement.p: The vectors \mathbf u=(3,1) and \mathbf v=(1,2) span a parallelogram. Evaluate (dx\wedge dy)(\mathbf u,\mathbf v) and (dx\wedge dy)(\mathbf v,\mathbf u). Explain why reversing the ordered pair changes signed area but leaves ordinary area unchanged.

hint.p: Use u_1v_2-u_2v_1, then interchange \mathbf u and \mathbf v. Ordinary area is the absolute value of the signed result.

subsection.p: This chapter began with Hamilton trying to multiply directions. It ends with a different kind of product, one that does not try to turn area into a vector. It lets area be area. Before these forms become integrals, one more piece of machinery has to arrive. We need rules that move every vector in a grid at once. Those rules are linear maps, and their bookkeeping devices are matrices.
